name: Sofia's body clock and morning light

parameters.label: Bright light each day
parameters.explain: Bright light reaching the eyes in the morning moves the body clock earlier, so sleepiness arrives earlier in the evening.

parameters.label: When the bright light comes
parameters.explain: The twist dial: the same bright light late in the evening pushes the clock the other way — later, and by even more.

parameters.label: Days of the routine
parameters.explain: Each morning nudges the clock a little, so the change builds up over days rather than happening on the first night.

parameters.label: How tired practice makes her
parameters.explain: Test the 'practice tires her out' idea: being tired helps her drop off a few minutes sooner, but it doesn't move her body clock.

parameters.label: How bright her mornings are
parameters.explain: The brain's master clock responds to the amount of light the eyes receive; outdoor daylight is far brighter than indoor lamps.

parameters.label: Her night-owl drift
parameters.explain: During the teen years the body starts making its sleep hormone later, so the clock tends to slide later unless something pulls it back.

outputs.label: Lying awake after a 10:30 p.m. bedtime

explain.summary: Sofia's brain has a master clock that decides when her sleep hormone, melatonin, arrives. Light reaching her eyes sets that clock. Bright light in the morning nudges it earlier — about a quarter of an hour each day — while her teenage clock keeps trying to slide later. Two weeks of sunrise practice add up to a clock that's about two and a half hours earlier, so she's sleepy by 10:30.
rules: An hour of bright morning light moves the clock about 15 minutes earlier each day.
Dimmer light moves it less; bright light late in the evening moves it later instead.
Her teenage clock slides back a few minutes each day, so only the difference adds up.
Feeling sleepy comes earlier by the same amount the clock moves.
Being tired from practice only shortens the time it takes to drop off.

source.fact: Bright morning light causes a phase advance, so people get sleepy earlier in the evening; bright evening light causes a delay. Morning light can shift the clock about 1 hour earlier per day and evening light about 2 hours later.
A single 1-hour bright-light pulse on waking moved the clock about 15 minutes earlier on average; individual responses varied widely.

The brain's master clock controls melatonin based on the amount of light the eyes receive; in the evening it makes more melatonin, causing sleepiness. Light and dark have the biggest influence on circadian rhythms.
Teenagers develop a strong tendency to be night owls because their bodies start producing melatonin later; teens need 8 to 10 hours of sleep.

choice.what: An hour of bright morning light moves the clock 15 minutes a day
choice.why: This matches the average 1-hour light pulse; it is well under the 1-hour-a-day maximum.

choice.what: Her clock slides back 4 minutes a day
choice.why: Teen clocks tend to run late; with this drift, two weeks of practice moves her sleepy time from 1 a.m. to about 10:30 p.m., matching clue 4.

choice.what: Evening light pushes the clock later by twice as much
choice.why: Evening light can shift the clock about 2 hours later a day, versus about 1 hour earlier for morning light.

choice.what: Practice tiredness only shortens the 20 minutes it takes to drop off
choice.why: Tiredness builds sleep pressure, but clue 1 shows it didn't move her bedtime — the dial lets you check that.

choice.what: Days add up in a straight line
choice.why: Over two weeks a steady routine adds a similar nudge each day; real clocks settle once they line up with the light.

illustrative: Sofia is fictional; her 1 a.m. sleepy time, her drift and the lying-awake minutes are teaching values.
provenance.studying: Scientists are still working out how much the teenage shift toward later sleep comes from biology and how much from evening light and schedules.

citations.title: Module 2. Effects of Light on Circadian Rhythms (NIOSH training for nurses on shift work and long hours)
citations.supports: Bright morning light causes a phase advance (sleepy earlier in the evening); bright evening light causes a phase delay. Evening light can shift the circadian system about 2 hours later per day; morning light about 1 hour earlier per day.

citations.title: The Phase Response Curve (PRC)
citations.supports: Light on awakening advances the clock and light around bedtime delays it; a single 1-hour 8,000-lux white-light pulse on waking gave an average advance of about 15 minutes; individual responses varied widely.

citations.title: Circadian Rhythms
citations.publisher: NIH National Institute of General Medical Sciences
citations.supports: The master clock controls production of melatonin based on the amount of light the eyes receive; in the evening it tells the brain to make more melatonin, causing sleepiness; light and dark have the biggest influence on circadian rhythms.

citations.title: Teens and Sleep
citations.supports: Adolescents develop a strong tendency toward being a night owl as the body starts producing melatonin later in the day; teens aged 13 to 18 are recommended 8 to 10 hours of sleep per night.

does: Shows bright morning light moving the body clock earlier
Shows the shift building over days of the routine
Shows an earlier clock meaning less time lying awake at night
doesnt: Measure any real person — Sofia is fictional
Include caffeine, stress or weekend lie-ins
Say anything about sleep problems; everyone's clock drifts sometimes
limits.text: This is a simplified learning model. Real people vary with age, fitness and health. The numbers are illustrative, not measurements of any real person.
limits.wellbeing: If you're exhausted every day no matter what you try, talk with an adult you trust.
